paper_title: Skill$^{\infty}$: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which a system also improves the way it improves, is a long-standing aspiration on the path to AGI. Language agents increasingly store procedural knowledge in reusable skills. Optimizing skills offers a direct way to achieve RSI, because the optimization procedure itself can be encoded as a skill. Existing skill optimizers, however, follow a hand-designed procedure. Even methods that evolve a meta-skill confine it to a fixed pipeline and relearn it for each task. We present Skill$^{\infty}$, which makes skill optimization recursively self-improving: a meta agent follows a meta-skill to optimize task skills and optimizes the meta-skill itself using the same procedure. The optimization is agent-led. The meta agent diagnoses execution traces, proposes candidates, requests independent reviews, and allocates the search budget. The meta-skill defines these steps, allowing self-improvement to rewrite them. This meta-skill is also decoupled from task skills, refined on multiple skill optimization tasks and then reused to optimize task skills across diverse domains. As in deployment, skills at both levels are standard packages loaded through native skill discovery. On 83 SkillsBench tasks, Skill$^{\infty}$ reaches a pass rate of 60.7%, compared with 56.4% for human-curated skills and 54.5% for SkillEvolver.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) refers to system that improves not only its performance on tasks but also the procedure that produces these improvements (Yudkowsky, 2007; Chen et al., 2026). Because each gain can then accelerate the next, RSI has figured prominently in visions of artificial general intelligence (AGI), from the intelligence explosion envisioned by Good (1966) *Corresponding author. Code will be released at https: //github.com/taowangcheng/Skill-Infinity. 1 to Gödel machines (Schmidhuber, 2003). More recently, skills have emerged as common format for capturing the reusable procedural knowledge of language agents (Anthropic, 2025b). This format can also encode the procedure that optimizes skills. Skills can thus encode both the target of improvement and the procedure that improves it, making skill optimization direct and interpretable way to achieve RSI. Skills also serve as harness-agnostic medium for RSI, since Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025a), Codex (OpenAI, 2025), and OpenCode (Anomaly, 2025) all load them through the same open specification (Agent Skills, 2025). To realize this potential, skill optimization must improve not only skills but also the procedure that optimizes them. Recent approaches such as SkillOpt (Yang et al., 2026), CoEvoSkills (Zhang et al., 2026b), and SkillEvolver (Zhang et al., 2026a) already optimize skills from execution feedback. Despite differences in what they edit and how they verify candidates, these methods share one design choice. The optimizer follows hand-designed procedure, and what it learns while optimizing one skill does not transfer to the next. MetaSkill-Evolve (Wang et al., 2026b) goes step further: each search branch carries meta-skill that configures the five agents of its pipeline, and the same pipeline refines this meta-skill. However, the pipelines roles and wiring remain fixed, and each meta-skill is bound to the task skill it evolves with. Some methods also optimize skills in setting that differs from deployment (Yang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b). They inject the skill or prompt the agent to load it, so optimization never tests whether the agent would load the skill on its own. We believe that an optimizer that improves skills but not its own procedure will eventually stagnate. RSI targets exactly this limitation. In this work, we propose Skill, framework for recursively selfimproving skill optimization. meta agent follows Prior methods: Optimizer Skill Hand-designed procedure Meta-skill Skill Evolving in fixed pipeline Bound to one skill Skill: m1 Meta-skill optimizes itself m s0 Meta-skill optimizes task skills s1 meta-skill/ SKILL.md Complete one iteration Analyze the rollout Interpret scores references/ workspace.md evoctl.md reviewer-policy.md scripts/ archive.py Figure 1: Recursively self-improving skill optimization. Left: most skill optimizers follow hand-designed procedure. Methods that evolve meta-skill keep it inside fixed pipeline and bound to the task skill it evolves with. Center: the shape shows the two loops of Skill, which meet at the meta-skill. In the left loop, the meta-skill optimizes itself on set of skill optimization tasks, improving from m0 to m. In each stacked loop on the right, the refined meta-skill is reused to optimize one task skill from s0 to s. Right: the meta-skill at the crossing is standard skill package loaded through native skill discovery, like any other skill. Each of its parts, from instructions to scripts, falls within the scope of self-improvement. meta-skill to optimize task skills and applies the same procedure to the meta-skill itself. The in Skill stands for two loops that meet at the meta-skill and feed into each other, as illustrated in Figure 1. Optimization in Skill is agent-led: in each iteration, the meta agent diagnoses the parent skill from execution traces, proposes and evaluates candidates within the search budget, submits each candidate to an independent reviewer, and selects the next parent. Self-improvement of the meta-skill refines this procedure, which in turn optimizes task skills more effectively. We further decouple the meta-skill from task skills. The meta-skill is refined on set of skill optimization tasks and then reused to optimize diverse task skills. This decoupling amortizes the cost of self-improvement over task skill optimization. Skills at both levels are also provided to agents through native skill discovery, as in deployment. We neither inject skill nor prompt an agent to load one. Agents see only skills name and description and decide whether to load it. The description is therefore also included in the scope of optimization. We evaluate Skill on 83 agentic tasks from SkillsBench (Li et al., 2026a), spanning eight domains, and on GPU kernel optimization from In the KernelBench (Ouyang et al., 2025). main comparison, all methods share the Codex CLI (OpenAI, 2025) as the harness and GPT-6 Luna (OpenAI, 2026b) as the backbone model. On SkillsBench, Skill reaches pass rate of 60.7%, compared with 56.4% for human-curated skills and 54.5% for SkillEvolver, and on KernelBench it reaches mean speedup of 1.62. Without the selfimprovement of the meta-skill, the pass rate falls to 55.9%. Skill still outperforms human-curated skills when the backbone model or the harness is replaced. Case studies in Appendix show that self-improvement changes how the meta agent acts, not only the wording of its instructions.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Recursive Self-Improvement The idea of RSI dates back to the argument for an intelligence explosion (Good, 1966). Gödel machines (Schmidhuber, 2003) later formalized it as program that rewrites its own code once rewrite is proven useful. Long vision of AGI, RSI has since been partly realized in agents built on language models. STOP (Zelikman et al., 2024) runs code-improving scaffold on its own code but notes that this is not full RSI, because the language model itself is not altered. Research on selfevolving agents (Gao et al., 2026) has introduced systems that rewrite their own logic or code (Yin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026c; Wang et al., 2026a) or search over agent designs (Hu et al., 2025). More recent systems make the meta-level modification procedure itself editable (Zhang et al., 2026d) or compose data, harness, and model updates (Tan et al., 2026). R2 Flow (Zhang et al., 2026e) trains policy that orchestrates skill library and commits verified edits to it. These systems implement the optimizer as program or trained policy. Skill, however, encodes the optimizers procedure as skill, which makes its recursive self-improvement direct, interpretable, and harness-agnostic. 2 Agent Skills and Skill Optimization Agent skills package reusable procedures as portable directories that agents load on demand (Anthropic, 2025b; Agent Skills, 2025; Xu and Yan, 2026). libraries, This format has precedents in skill induced workflows, and programmatic web skills (Wang et al., 2024, 2025b,a; Zheng et al., 2025). growing line of work learns skills from experience (Ni et al., 2026; Xia et al., 2026) or optimizes them from execution feedback (Alzubi et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026b; Tian et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b; Feng et al., 2026). SkillEvolver (Zhang et al., 2026a) writes its optimization procedure as fixed meta-skill that audits candidate skills in separate agents. Some methods go further and operate at the meta level, evolving meta-skills that guide skill optimization (Wang et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026b), multiagent system design (Lin et al., 2026a), or context engineering (Ye et al., 2026). These methods still evolve the meta-skill with hand-designed procedure. MetaSkill-Evolve (Wang et al., 2026b), for instance, fixes the roles and wiring of its fiveagent pipeline and binds each meta-skill to the task skill it evolves with. Skill instead writes an agentled optimization procedure into the meta-skill and refines it through self-improvement on several skill optimization tasks. Decoupled from task skills, the same meta-skill then optimizes diverse task skills. Prompt and Context Optimization Skill optimization builds on prompt optimization. Early methods select instructions that language model proposes (Zhou et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024) or evolve populations of prompts (Guo et al., 2024; Fernando et al., 2024). Subsequent methods optimize compound systems of model calls (Yuksekgonul et al., 2025; Khattab et al., 2024; Agrawal et al., 2026), accumulate strategies in evolving contexts (Suzgun et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026f), or meta-learn system prompts that transfer across tasks (Choi et al., 2025; Tao et al., 2026). These methods optimize text that the surrounding system inserts into the models context. By contrast, Skill optimizes skills, which bundle executable scripts and reference files, are loaded only when the agent judges them useful, and can even package the procedure that optimizes them.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: We first formalize skills, native skill discovery, and task skill optimization by meta-skill. We then make the meta-skill an optimization target in its own right, so that single agent-led procedure optimizes task skills and the meta-skill alike. Finally, we decouple the meta-skill from task skills and extend native skill discovery to both levels.

sections.title: 3.1 Preliminaries
sections.content: Skill Packages and Native Skill Discovery We adopt the Agent Skills specification (Agent Skills, 2025), an open format through which agents across harnesses share reusable procedural knowledge. skill package is directory built around the SKILL.md file. The front matter of SKILL.md declares the skills name and description, while the body holds the instructions. The package may also bundle scripts, reference files, and other resources that the instructions invoke or cite. With these resources, skill can provide executable procedures and detailed conventions in addition to textual guidance. An agent loads skills in stages, following design principle known as progressive disclosure (Anthropic, 2025b). Initially, it sees only the name and description of each installed skill. For skill it judges useful for the current task, it then loads the full instructions and opens the bundled resources as needed. skill thus takes effect only when the agent activates it by loading its instructions. We term this mechanism native skill discovery because it is built into agent harnesses and underlies skill use during deployment. Tasks and Task Skills task τ consists of an instruction, an environment, and verifier that returns scalar reward for each trial, one execution by task agent. task agent is an agent harness with backbone model and an installed task skill s. The score of on set of tasks is the mean reward over trials per task, macro-averaged across tasks: S(s; ) = 1 (cid:88) τ 1 (cid:88) j=1 rj(s, τ ), (1) where rj(s, τ ) is the reward of the j-th trial on task τ with skill s. Task Skill Optimization by Meta-Skill Given seed task skill s0 and set of tasks , task skill optimization seeks skill that maximizes the score on test tasks. Our optimizer is meta agent built on the same harness and backbone model as the task agent rather than stronger one. Its procedure is itself skill: the meta agent follows meta-skill m, skill package whose instructions describe how to optimize skills.

The agent-led procedure of Section 3.3 therefore applies directly to the meta-skill itself. 4 The Recursive Loop When the meta-skill improves itself, it is both the procedure that the meta agent follows and the target that this procedure optimizes. The meta agent thus diagnoses and revises this procedure while following it. The revised metaskill is then evaluated on skill optimization tasks, where the optimizations it guides reveal whether it surpasses the predecessor. Such loop makes selfimprovement recursive, since improvements to the meta-skill are self-reinforcing. Each strengthens the procedure from which further improvements arise, yielding an increasingly capable meta-skill.

sections.title: 3.3 Agent-Led Optimization
sections.content: Anatomy of an Iteration We place the meta agent at the helm of skill optimization, following meta-skill that is editable by self-improvement. Algorithm 1 outlines the procedure, and Figure 2 depicts one of its iterations. The meta agent first inspects the optimization history recorded in the archive. It then diagnoses the parent skill from the execution traces of its rollouts. Informed by this diagnosis, it creates one or two candidates from the parent, each justified by proposal. Finally, it decides whether to continue and selects either the next parent or the optimized skill. Search as Reasoning Agent-led optimization entrusts the search to the meta agents reasoning rather than to hand-designed heuristic driven by scores. score reveals whether candidate improved but not why, so the meta agent interprets it in light of the diagnoses and reviews recorded in the archive. The diagnoses can uncover promising change that the score has yet to reflect, such as tied candidate that makes progress on the failure it targets. Much as evolutionary search retains less fit candidates to escape local optima, the meta agent can build on such candidates instead of discarding them. It may likewise keep the parent when candidates gain cannot be attributed to its change, or backtrack to an earlier skill when line of revisions stalls. Beyond choosing parents, the meta agent decides which failures to address next, redirecting the search as new evidence emerges. In sum, search becomes reasoning about the failure modes of each target skill rather than heuristic applied to all. Independent Review Only candidates that pass an independent review are eligible for selection. The reviewer operates in an isolated context, shielded from both the meta agents deliberation and its partiality toward its own changes. The verdict rests solely on the parent and candidate packages, the proposal, and the supporting evidence. The reviewer rejects candidates that make no substantive change, that are never activated, or that are unusable as written. Any gain from such candidates can arise only by chance, and rejecting them prevents selection from mistaking noise for progress. For meta-skill candidate, the reviewer further verifies that the core responsibilities of meta-skill, including the review itself, remain intact. Adaptive Budget Allocation The meta agent allocates the search budget itself, deciding how many candidates to create in each iteration and when to stop. The number of candidates per iteration sets the balance between exploration and exploitation. Several candidates probe alternative revisions side by side, whereas single candidate pursues one line of revisions in depth. Across target skills, fixed schedule would allocate the same budget regardless of how much headroom remains. The meta agent instead adapts its spending to each target skill, continuing while failures persist and stopping once the diagnosis finds little left to improve. End-to-End RSI The steps of Algorithm 1 are encoded in the meta-skill rather than hard-coded, so the recursive loop of Section 3.2 can rewrite the procedure itself. Any part of the package, from the instructions to the bundled scripts, is open to revision. Freed from any predefined design space, the procedure can evolve beyond the foresight of human designers and realize its full potential. Selfimprovement can remedy weak step wherever it lies, even in the review and selection of candidates, which fixed pipeline would leave untouched. Optimizing task skills reveals the shortcomings of the procedure, and each refinement in turn yields better task skills, rendering the two levels mutually reinforcing. To keep the mutual reinforcement genuine, scoring lies beyond the reach of selfimprovement, so gains can arise only from better optimization, never from reward tampering.

This decoupling separates concerns: the metaskill captures how to optimize skills, and each task skill how to solve its tasks. Averaging gains over Q, the meta score favors revisions that help across domains over those tailored to one. As standard skill package, the refined meta-skill serves all task skills optimized afterwards, amortizing the cost of self-improvement across them.

sections.title: 3.5 Native Skill Discovery at Both Levels
sections.content: Skills at both levels are installed in the harnesss standard skill location and loaded through native skill discovery, as in deployment. No skill is injected into prompt, nor is any agent instructed to load one. Gains measured under these conditions need no injection to materialize in deployment. For task skills and the meta-skill alike, activation thus hinges on the description, which joins the instructions within the scope of optimization. Like any skill, the meta-skill is portable across harnesses that support native skill discovery.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate Skill on SkillsBench (Li et al., 2026a) and KernelBench (Ouyang et al., 2025) against baselines with and without skills. Beyond the main results, we ablate self-improvement and test generality across harnesses and models. We further locate where Skill helps and measure how performance scales with the search budget and what optimization costs.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Benchmarks SkillsBench quantifies how much skills improve agent performance across diverse agentic tasks by pairing each task with humancurated skills. We optimize task skills on the dataset released with SkillEvolver (Zhang et al., 2026a) and test them on its 83 SkillsBench tasks from eight domains. KernelBench challenges an agent to replace PyTorch reference model with faster implementation that computes the same outputs. Following SkillEvolver, we optimize one task skill shared across three level-3 problems whose reference models are deep narrow MLP, ShuffleNet, and GRU. Baselines All baselines use the same harness and backbone model as Skill. No skill and Human-curated evaluate the task agent without skill and with the human-curated skills Self-generated of SkillsBench, respectively. asks the task agent to write its own skills before using them to solve the task (Li et al., SkillCreator authors skill with 2026a). Anthropics skill-creator (Anthropic, 2025c), which CoEvoSkills (Zhang et al., 2026b) adapted to run without human interaction. SkillEvolver (Zhang et al., 2026a) uses its released meta-skill to author, deploy, and revise skill over two rounds. Configurations The main experiments use the Codex CLI (OpenAI, 2025) with GPT-6 Luna (OpenAI, 2026b) at high reasoning effort, and Harbor (Harbor Framework Team, 2026) executes the trials. Seed task skills are instantiated from the template in Appendix F, which identifies the task but carries no task-specific guidance. We measure the search budget in candidates and cap it at four per task skill. For self-improvement, the meta agent refines the seed meta-skill in Appendix on skill optimization tasks drawn from different domains, with the budgets given in Appendix B. We choose tasks that the seed task skill has not saturated, since saturated task offers no gain by which stronger meta-skill could distinguish itself. Metrics As in SkillEvolver, we evaluate performance on SkillsBench by avg@5, the pass rate over five trials per task. The metric counts trial as passed when its reward is positive. On KernelBench, we report the correctness-weighted speedup, which is the speedup over the PyTorch reference for correct implementation and zero for an incorrect one. All reported results are averaged over 5 independent runs.

sections.title: 4.5 Where Skill∞ Helps
sections.content: An overall pass rate does not show which tasks benefit from Skill. Following SkillEvolver (Zhang et al., 2026a), we group tasks by skill utility as defined in Appendix A. Category holds tasks that the agent solves without skill. B1, B2, and B3 hold partly solved tasks on which human-curated skills improve, preserve, or degrade the pass rate, respectively. C1 and C2 hold tasks that only humancurated skills solve, at pass rates of at least 40% and below 40%, respectively. holds tasks that neither the agent alone nor human-curated skills solve. Table 2 reports the pass rate per category. The improvements of Skill concentrate on tasks beyond the agents reach. On tasks that neither the agent nor human-curated skills solve (D), Skill reaches 30.5%, against 22.1% for SkillEvolver. On tasks that only human-curated skills solve at pass rate of at least 40% (C1), Skill reaches 29.2%, against 15.4% for SkillEvolver. Skill provides the procedural knowledge that the agent lacks, even on tasks that human-curated skills fail to solve.

sections.title: 4.6 Budget Scaling and Amortized Cost
sections.content: Scaling the Search Budget We ask whether larger budget yields further gains, given that the meta agent allocates the budget itself. We run this analysis on subset of tasks, where the default budget substantially improves the seed task skill. We then optimize their task skills with budgets of one, two, and eight candidates under otherwise identical settings. As shown in Figure 5, the pass rate rises with each doubling of the budget, from 47.5% with one candidate to 82.5% with eight. Even with single candidate, the optimized task skills far exceed the agent without skill (12.5%). The meta agent allocates each budget itself, so these gains 8 ) % ( r a 100 80 60 40 0 default 1 2 4 Search budget (candidates) No skill 8 Figure 5: Pass rate under different search budgets. Test pass rate (avg@5, %) on subset of SkillsBench tasks. The solid line shows the optimized task skills, and the dashed line the agent without skill. require no retuning of the procedure. Agent-led optimization scales with the search budget. Cost We measure cost by the tokens that all agents consume during optimization, as itemized in Appendix E. Optimizing task skill with the refined meta-skill requires 8.7M input and 66k output tokens on average, close to 8.1M and 76k for SkillEvolver. The cost of self-improvement is amortized across all task skills optimized afterwards. Self-improvement consumes about as many tokens as eleven task skill optimizations. Spread over the 83 task skills, this cost adds less than 15% to each optimization, share that shrinks with each further reuse of the meta-skill. By reusing its refined meta-skill, Skill surpasses SkillEvolver at comparable cost.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: followed handSkill optimizers have so far designed procedures. Even methods that evolve meta-skill fix the pipeline around it and relearn it for each task. We presented Skill, which makes skill optimization recursively self-improving. meta agent follows meta-skill to optimize task skills, and the same agent-led procedure optimizes the meta-skill itself. The meta-skill, decoupled from task skills, is refined on skill optimization tasks and then reused to optimize task skills across domains. At both levels, agents load their skills through native skill discovery, as in deployment. On SkillsBench, Skill outperforms humancurated skills and SkillEvolver, and it improves kernel speedups on KernelBench. Encoding the optimizers procedure as skill makes recursive self-improvement direct, interpretable, and harnessagnostic. We hope that this view invites further work on agents that improve the way they improve.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Skill makes skill optimization recursively selfimproving while the backbone model stays fixed. The resulting gains are therefore bounded by the expressiveness of skill packages. Both levels of optimization rely on automatic verifiers, since the meta score is computed from task rewards. Skill therefore applies to domains in which such rewards can be computed reliably. Finally, agent-led optimization trades enforcement for flexibility. The meta agent follows its procedure rather than executing it as code. The effect of the meta-skill thus depends on how reliably the backbone model follows long instructions. No tool enforces this adherence, which rests instead on the meta-skill and on independent review.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: Optimized skills bundle instructions and executable scripts that agents follow with tool access, and an agent may activate them without user approval. We therefore recommend reviewing what these skills do and when they are activated before deploying them. Some SkillsBench tasks concern cybersecurity and are used only in the form the benchmark provides. sections.title: C Case Studies
sections.content: The Meta-Skill Rewrites Its Selection Rule During self-improvement, the meta agent diagnosed the seed meta-skill from the inner optimizations it had guided. For the 3D scene task, the inner optimization had accepted two consecutive candidates while the verifier still reported the same link-geometry failure. It had also selected the second candidate, which only tied the parent. The meta agent located this weakness in the inspection and selection of evaluated candidates rather than in diagnosis. The candidate meta-skill it wrote requires checking the rollout of each tied or worse candidate for the targeted failure. tied candidate can then be selected only when that rollout shows progress. The candidate improved the meta score from 0.55 to 0.83. In the next iteration, the meta agent followed this candidate and proposed further change that tracks intermediate scores and verifier failures across candidates. The new candidate tied its parent. Applying the rule it had just written, the meta agent selected the tied candidate only after checking its inner optimization on the 3D scene task. There, the targeted failure had been addressed, and the task skill had reached perfect score. Self-improvement then stopped after two further candidates and retained this candidate as the refined meta-skill. Across the 83 task skill optimizations, the refined meta-skill selected 54% of tied candidates, against 83% for the seed meta-skill. Self-improvement changes the behavior of the meta agent, not merely the text of its instructions. Task Skill Gains Script For SkillsBench task that exports the parts of Three.js scene as OBJ files, the seed task skill fails all test trials. In the first iteration, rollout of the seed showed that each individual mesh passed while merged link file failed the verifiers geometry check. The meta agent attributed this failure to group ownership and coordinate transforms. It added an exporter script, wrote the ownership and transform rules into SKILL.md, and rewrote the description to specify the files the skill produces. Its proposal states falsifying outcome in terms of the verifiers check. The reviewer confirmed that the script exists and matches the documented interface before accepting the candidate. The optimized skill passes all five test trials. The boxes below show the optimized task skill and its proposal.
